CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Retaliate in kind to the $50B tariffs already imposed and the pending List 2, while signaling willingness to negotiate through diplomatic channels. Do not escalate beyond matching retaliation. Use targeted agricultural and energy tariffs to create political pressure in US farm-belt states. Tolerate orderly yuan depreciation as a natural shock absorber but do not weaponize it. Accelerate domestic fiscal support for affected export sectors and fast-track Made in China 2025 investment to reduce long-term dependency on US technology.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat reading of +0.65 reflects a rapidly escalating situation that poses a serious but not yet existential threat to China's export economy. The US has moved from $34B in tariffs (effective July 6) to proposing $200B in List 3 tariffs and considering raising the rate from 10% to 25% (Aug 1 USTR announcement). If all lists materialize, ~$250B of Chinese exports face tariffs—roughly half of the ~$500B annual exports to the US. JP Morgan analysts warned (July 2018) that indirect effects on business sentiment, investment, and growth could cause 'large' collateral damage, and that the timing is particularly bad as China was finally addressing credit growth. The yuan has depreciated ~7% since mid-April (from ~6.3 to ~6.9 per dollar), partly absorbing tariff costs but raising capital flight risks—the same dynamic that cost China ~$1T in reserves during the 2015-16 depreciation. The ZTE episode (April ban, July resolution with $1.4B penalty) demonstrated acute vulnerability in China's tech supply chain, with ZTE forced to nearly shut down because it could not source US chips and software. This validates the urgency of Made in China 2025 but also underscores that self-sufficiency is years away.

However, the situation is not yet existential: GDP remains at 6.8% in H1 2018, foreign reserves are substantial, and China has fiscal room to absorb the shock. The US economy is showing strain (consumer sentiment down 5.1% from March to August, from 101.4 to 96.2), which limits US domestic appetite for prolonged escalation. The action stance of -0.25 (retaliate, mild) reflects the calculus that China must signal resolve—both domestically and internationally—without triggering a further escalation spiral. China imports far less from the US (~$130B) than it exports (~$500B), so symmetric retaliation is impossible; targeting politically sensitive goods (soybeans, automobiles, energy) creates leverage by concentrating pain on US constituencies that matter to Trump's base. Full escalation would risk accelerating capital flight, triggering a broader Asian currency crisis, and providing justification for even more aggressive US action. The optimal path is calibrated retaliation combined with quiet diplomatic engagement.
key_factors: Rapid tariff escalation: $34B in effect, $16B pending, $200B proposed with rate raised to 25%
Yuan depreciation of ~7% since mid-April provides partial offset but carries capital flight risk
ZTE ban demonstrated acute tech supply chain vulnerability—China cannot yet replace US semiconductors
China's retaliation options are asymmetric: ~$130B imports vs ~$500B exports to US
JP Morgan warns of 'large' collateral damage from indirect effects on sentiment and investment
US consumer sentiment declining (101.4 → 96.2) limits US appetite for prolonged escalation
Made in China 2025 is the long-term answer but tech self-sufficiency is years away
Tension between deleveraging goals and need for growth-supporting monetary/fiscal response

sources_cited.excerpt: At Trump's direction, USTR says it is considering raising the proposed List 3 rate from 10% to 25%.
List 1 tariffs take effect: US 25% on ~$34B of Chinese goods. China imposes matching ~$34B retaliation the same day.
USTR publishes proposed List 3: ~$200B of Chinese imports for an additional 10% tariff (~6,000 product lines).
US Commerce Department bans ZTE from buying US components (denial order). ZTE faces operational shutdown.
White House announces the US will proceed with Section 301 actions. Truce collapses.
Consumer sentiment declined from 101.4 (March) to 96.2 (August), a drop of 5.1%.
Broad dollar index rose from ~107.6 (Feb) to ~115.2 (Aug), up ~7%, reflecting tightening financial conditions globally.

J.P. Morgan analysts: 'All this puts China in a very difficult position... the timing couldn't have been worse. After years of handwringing, China finally began to focus in earnest on curbing credit growth.'
The value of China's renminbi has fallen over 7 percent since mid-April. A lower renminbi makes China's exports cheaper to foreign buyers.
